topic: The Physics of Pi: Colliding Blocks and Numerical Discovery
target_audience: Undergraduate physics or computer science students

outline.topic: The Physics of Pi: Colliding Blocks and Numerical Discovery
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate physics or computer science students

sections.title: Introduction: The Unexpected Appearance of Pi
sections.content: Introduce the counter-intuitive puzzle: How can colliding blocks on a friction-less surface calculate the digits of Pi? Set the premise: two blocks of mass ratio 1:100^n colliding with a wall.
sections.example: Visualize a tiny mouse (Block A) and a giant elephant (Block B) sliding on ice, bouncing off each other and a wall.

sections.title: Prerequisite Physics: Conservation Laws
sections.content: Establish the foundational rules: Elastic collisions conserve both momentum (mv) and kinetic energy (1/2mv^2). Use graphical vectors to show velocity changes before and after impact.
sections.example: Use a billiard ball diagram to illustrate how the speed exchange happens during a perfect elastic bounce.

sections.title: The Mechanism: Mapping Collisions to Angles
sections.content: Introduce the 'Phase Space' concept. Explain that the state of the system (velocities of two blocks) can be represented as a vector in 2D space. The collision constraint acts like a circular boundary, causing the system to traverse a circular arc.
sections.example: A clock hand rotating on a circle; each collision represents a specific degree of rotation equivalent to the arc length.

sections.title: The Pi Connection: Geometric Interpretation
sections.content: Explain that as the mass ratio becomes infinitely large (1:100^n), the path of the velocities traces a full semicircle. The total number of collisions maps directly to the digits of Pi through the geometry of the circle's arc length.
sections.example: Animation showing the velocity vector traversing a semicircle, where the 'bounces' mark the division of the circumference.

sections.title: Conclusion and Real-World Application
sections.content: Summarize how discrete physical interactions can compute transcendental numbers. Emphasize that Pi is not just about circles, but about the fundamental symmetry of conservation laws.
sections.example: Show a digital counter on a computer screen that ticks up every time the 'blocks' collide, slowly revealing '3.1415...' as the total collision count.
